parsed.attack: Heritage-language regret is the textbook case of a pain that is stated intensely and acted on never: second-generation adults have had free family tutors in the next room for thirty years, plus Duolingo, Memrise and countless Punjabi and Gujarati courses, and have not learned - the obstacle is shame, and the fact that the grandmother switches to English within two exchanges to spare everyone. The wedge makes this worse by putting the hardest emotional act first: before any value is delivered, the user must ask their grandmother to sit and record fifty phrases, which is a more intimate and awkward conversation than the one the app exists to enable. Anyone who completes that recording session has already had the connection the product promises and no longer needs the drill; everyone else churns at setup. A 25% day-30 retention kill threshold is above what Duolingo achieves with a decade of gamification and billions in spend, and it is set against a product with no streak pressure from a peer group.
parsed.strongest_defence: The recording session is not a barrier but the product - it is a reason to call, most families have hours of grandparents' voices already sitting in WhatsApp voice notes that can be mined without asking anyone for anything, and the acuteness the dead language apps lacked is mortality: a named grandmother in her eighties is a deadline that generic fluency never had.
parsed.verdict_reason: The audience's decades-long failure to act on an intensely stated desire is the purest say-do gap in the batch, though a specific named person and a closing window is a genuinely sharper trigger than fluency.
